04_marg1037: Morally. First I wish to ask who is the king in Egypt who knows Joseph, and who does not. For while he reigned who knew Joseph, the children of Israel are not said to have been afflicted, nor worn out in clay and brick, nor their males killed and the females kept alive; but when he began to reign who did not know Joseph. If the Lord rules us, and the sense of our mind or soul is enlightened by God, remembering that Christ rose from the dead, in Egypt, that is, in our flesh, our spirit holds the kingdom with justice, and does not wear out the children of Israel, that is, the rational senses or the virtues, in clay and brick, nor grind them down with earthly cares. If our sense loses the memory of these things and does not know Christ, then “the wisdom of the flesh,” which “is an enemy to God,” succeeds to the kingdom. It addresses its people, that is, the bodily pleasures, and, calling the leaders of the vices to counsel, deliberates against the children of Israel how they may be got round, oppressed, afflicted with clay and brick; how they may expose the males and rear the females; how they may build the cities of Egypt and its fortified cities. Nor is it to be thought that the divine books tell the deeds of the Egyptians without cause; but “what things were written, were written for our learning”; so that you who hear these things, if perhaps you are baptized and numbered among the children of Israel, and have received the Lord as king in yourself, and after this wish to turn aside and do the works of the world, to carry out the deeds of the earth and the services of clay, may know that another king has risen in you who does not know Joseph, a king of Egypt. He compels you to his works, to work brick and clay. He, with masters and taskmasters set over you, drives you with whips to earthly works, so that you may build cities for him. He makes you run about the world, troubling the elements of sea and land for greed; beat at the courts with lawsuits; weary your neighbours with quarrels for a little turf of land; lay snares for chastity, deceive innocence, commit foul things at home, cruel things abroad, shameful things within the conscience. In things of this kind know that you are serving as a soldier of the king of Egypt, which is to be driven by the spirit of this world.

04_marg1038: Therefore he set over them masters, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. The devil, having called his people together, desires to oppress the rational sense, which is now called Israel in figure. He set over them masters of works, to compel them to learn the works of the flesh; according to that: “They were mingled among the heathens, and learned their works.” He teaches them to build cities for Pharao: Phithom, which signifies “mouth of failing” or “of the abyss”; and Ramesses, which is “the stirring of the moth”; and On, that is, Heliopolis, which is called the city of the sun. The mouth fails from truth and proofs when it speaks a lie. He was a liar from the beginning, and therefore wishes such cities to be built for him. “Mouth of the abyss,” because the abyss is the place of his perdition. His other city is “the stirring of the moth.” For whoever follows him lays up treasure where the moth destroys and thieves break through and steal. He builds also the city of the sun, under a false name, because “he transformeth himself into an angel of light.” In these he busies the minds that were made to see God. Yet he foresees that wars threaten him and that the ruin of his people is ripe. Therefore he says: “The people of Israel is stronger than we.” Would that he might feel us too to be stronger than he: that is, that I may not receive the evil thoughts and desires he sends in, but drive back his fiery darts with the shield of faith, and in all that he suggests say: “Begone, Satan; for it is written: The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve.” And as for his saying, “Lest perhaps a war befall us, and these side with our adversaries”: from the prophetic voices he foresees the war to come, and that he must be forsaken by the children of Israel, and that they will side with his adversary and be added to the Lord. This is what Jeremias says: “The partridge hath cried, she hath gathered together what she did not bring forth; he hath gathered riches, and not by right; in the midst of his days he shall leave them, and in his latter end he shall be a fool.” So he understands that he is the partridge that gathered what she did not bring forth, and that those whom he gathered without right will leave him and follow Christ, who begot them. He will remain a fool, when the whole creation flees to its maker and parent. Therefore he is indignant, saying: “Lest, overcoming us, they go out of our land.” He does not wish us to go out of his land, so that we may always bear the image of the earthly; lest, leaving him, we flee to him who has prepared the kingdom of heaven, leaving “the image of the earthly” and taking up “the image of the heavenly.” Therefore he set up masters of works, to teach their arts and make us craftsmen of malice. And because there are many masters of malice whom Pharao set over us, who command, exact and wring out earthly works, therefore, when Christ came, he made other teachers fighting against them, who, subduing all their principalities, powers and virtues, might defend the children of Israel from violence, and teach them the works of Israel and to see God with the mind; to leave the works of Pharao, to go out of the land of Egypt, to put off the ways of Egypt and the whole old man with his deeds, and to put on the new, who according to God is created.

04_marg1040: And the king of Egypt spoke, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. We find these things not only in the world, which is spiritually called Egypt, but in each one of us. The prince of this world does not wish the males to be kept alive, but the females. In the female the flesh and the affections of the flesh are signified; but the male is the rational sense and the intellectual spirit, which can grasp heavenly things, understand God, seek the things that are above. This the prince of Egypt hates and desires to be killed; but he desires the things of the flesh to live, and what belongs to bodily matter, not only to live but to be increased and cultivated. For he wishes all to savour fleshly things, to seek temporal things and those upon the earth; that no one lift his eyes to heaven, no one ask whence he came here, no one remember his country, paradise. So when you see men leading their lives in pleasures, floating in luxury, giving themselves to feasts and lewdness, know that in them the king of Egypt is killing the males and keeping the females alive. But if he sees one in a thousand turned to God, lifting his eyes upward, seeking eternal things, hating delights and luxury, loving continence, this one Pharao desires to be killed as a male; he persecutes him, attacks him with a thousand engines; he hates such men, and does not let them live in Egypt. Hence it is that in this world the servants of God are held in contempt and exposed to insults; hence hatreds and persecutions are stirred up against them.
04_marg1041: ORIGEN. He tries also to corrupt the midwives, of whom one was called Sephora, that is, “sparrow,” the other Phua, that is, “red” or “modest”; through them he seeks to have the males killed and the females kept alive. “But the midwives feared God, and did not as he commanded them.” The midwives taught us beforehand to hold a certain form of rational learning. For midwives are physicians, and they tend both the males and the females being born. So common learning is rational knowledge, and it reaches almost every sense, instructs and tends all. If anyone in it is of manly mind, who wishes to seek heavenly things and pursue divine things, he will come, as one doctored and strong, more ready through these learnings to the understanding of divine things. For there is one, like the sparrow, which teaches loftier things and calls upward on the wings of rational teaching. The other, red or modest, is moral: it orders conduct, teaches modesty and uprightness. Yet to me, because Scripture says of them that they feared God and did not do the command of the king of Egypt, they seem to keep the figure of both Testaments; and Sephora, which is interpreted “sparrow,” seems to fit the Law, which is spiritual; and Phua, which is “red” or “modest,” to point to the Gospels, which are red with the blood of Christ and glow red through the whole world with the blood of the passion. By these, then, as by midwives, the souls that are born in the Church are tended, because all the medicines of learning are supplied from the Scriptures. Yet Pharao tries through them to kill the males, when he suggests heresies and wicked doctrines to those studious in the divine Scriptures. But the foundation of God stands firm. For the midwives fear God, that is, they teach the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. So what follows fits more aptly: because the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses. Which according to the letter has no consequence; for a house is not made because God is feared. But if you see how the Scriptures of the New and Old Testament, teaching the fear of God, make the houses of the Church and fill the whole world with houses of prayer, it will seem reasonably written. So these midwives, because they fear God, that is, teach the fear of God, do not do the command of the king of Egypt, but keep the males alive; and yet it is not said that they obeyed by keeping the females alive. And I say confidently: they do not keep the females alive. For neither vices nor luxury are taught in the Church, nor are sins nourished, which Pharao wants when he orders the females to be kept alive; but virtue alone is cultivated and nourished. But let us refer these things to each one. If you fear God, you do not do the command of the king of Egypt; for he commands you to live in delights and to covet present things. You, if you fear God and perform the office of a midwife, if you desire to bring salvation to your soul, keep the males alive; that is, you tend and nurse the inner man who is in you, and by good deeds and understandings gain eternal life.

04_marg1044: They answered, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether such lies are approved by divine authority, because it is written that God dealt well with the midwives. But whether God pardoned the lies for the sake of the mercy, or judged even the lie worthy of reward, is uncertain. For the midwives did one thing in keeping the little ones alive, another in lying to Pharao. In keeping them alive it was a work of mercy; but they used the lie for themselves, lest Pharao harm them, which could belong not to praise but to pardon. Nor is authority for lying given from this to those of whom it is said: “And in their mouth there was found no lie.” For the life of some, far below the profession of the saints, if it has these sins of lies, is borne with for its very progress and disposition, especially if they do not yet know how to wait for heavenly benefits, but are busied about earthly ones. But those whose “conversation is in heaven” I do not think ought to shape the measure of their tongue concerning truth and falsehood by the example of the midwives.
04_marg1045: GREGORY. Lying must be shunned with the greatest care, though it is of lighter guilt if someone lies in doing a kindness. But since it is written, “The mouth that belieth killeth the soul,” and “Thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie,” the perfect flee even this, so that not even anyone’s life is defended by their deceit, lest they harm their own soul while striving to profit another’s flesh; though we readily believe that this kind of sin is forgiven. For if any guilt whatever is purged by a following devout work, how much more easily is this wiped away, which piety, the mother of good work, accompanies? But many try to assert from the deceit of the midwives that this kind of lie is not a sin, because the Lord built them houses. In which recompense, rather, it is known what the guilt of a lie deserves. For the reward of their kindness, which could have been repaid in eternal life, was turned aside, for the guilt of the lie, into an earthly recompense; so that in their life, which they wished to protect by lying, they received the good they had done, and had no further reward of wages to wait for. For if it is weighed closely, they lied for love of the present life, not with the intention of a reward. For by sparing they tried to shield the life of the infants; by lying, their own.

04_marg1048: After this there went, etc. RABANUS. Hence Josephus says: But Amram, fearing that if caught he would fall to the king’s wrath, and himself perish with the boy and shut out the providence of God, decided rather to see to the boy’s safety in this way, and judged that this was the providence of hiding. He prepared a round vessel woven of withies, of about the size of a cradle, enough for the infant to lie in it roomily. Then they daubed it with pitch; for it is the nature of pitch to keep back the entry of water in wicker vessels. So putting the infant there, and setting it near the river, they left his safety to God. Now Thermuth was the king’s daughter. While she was playing by the bank of the river, seeing that vessel carried by the river, she ordered that cradle to be brought to her. When those who had been sent for this came with the cradle, she took it, and seeing the infant, rejoiced greatly at his size and beauty. For God used such care about Moses that by the very people who, because of his birth, had decreed to destroy the whole race of the Hebrews, he was held worthy of food and care. And Thermuth, the king’s daughter, ordered a woman to be brought to give the infant the breast. When he would not go to her breasts but shunned them, and did this with many women, Mary, standing by what was being done, as if she seemed to be standing among the others by chance, said: In vain, O queen, do you call these women to nurse the infant, who have no kinship with him. But if you order one of the Hebrew women to be brought, I think he will be able to take the breast as from one of his own tribe. And when she was thought to have spoken well, she ordered her to go and bring someone who could suckle him. And she, having received such leave, came back bringing her mother, known to no one. And the infant went gladly, as it were, to her breasts; and at the queen’s request the nursing of the boy was entrusted to her with all diligence. And according to the outcome of events the name was given him because he was saved from the river. For the Egyptians call water moy, and saved ses; so putting this together from both they gave him the name Moses, that is, “saved from the water.” Allegorically. The parents of Moses, whose faith and works the natural law adorned, are the patriarchs, from whom Moses himself and those who received the law of the letter were born. So Moses, born in his parents’ house, is hidden for three months, since the old law lay hidden among the Jewish people for three periods before the coming of Christ, that is, under the judges, under the kings, under the priests, until he came who gave the law and handed it over to the Gentiles through the whole breadth of the world, to be kept spiritually. And Pharao’s daughter is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which, though she now rejoices in a true parent, that is, God the Father, yet before, when she served idols, followed another father; of whom it was said to her by the divine voice in the Psalm: “Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline thy ear; and forget thy people and thy father’s house,” etc. So she went out of her father’s house and came to the waters of baptism, to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father’s house; and coming to baptism she received the law, which was then inside a basket of bulrushes, woven of many twigs or of papyrus and daubed with pitch and slime, because it was fouled, hemmed in by the cheap and earthly traditions of the Jews; until the Church took it up from the marshy and muddy places of fleshly senses, and within the halls of true wisdom and the royal roofs. It spent its infancy among its own, that is, among those who did not know how to understand it spiritually, a little thing and the food of sucklings. But when it came to the Church and was rightly understood through her, it was made stronger. What then is it that she who nursed the boy received wages from Pharao’s daughter, unless that the synagogue, with whom the law was born and nursed, received this wage from the Church: that it should no longer worship idols; seeing those from the Gentiles who had believed so turned to the Lord that they utterly rejected images and no longer worshipped them, it too is taught to blush at worshipping idols?
04_marg1049: And seeing him a goodly child, etc. ORIGEN. Allegorically. Pharao’s daughter is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, to whom it is said through the Prophet: “Forget thy people and thy father’s house, for the king hath greatly desired thy beauty.” This, then, is she who went out of her father’s house and came to the waters to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father’s house; and at once she received bowels of mercy and had pity on the infant. Coming into the marsh, she found Moses lying, exposed by his own people, and had him nursed. He is nursed among his own and spends his infancy there; grown stronger, he is brought to her and adopted as a son. Moses signifies the Law. So the Church, coming to the waters of baptism, received the Law shut in a thibis and daubed with pitch. Now a thibis is a covering woven of papyrus and twigs, or formed from the bark of trees. So the Law lay shut within coverings of this kind, daubed with pitch and slime, that is, with the cheap and foul senses of the Jews; it lay fouled and smeared until the Church came from the Gentiles and took it up from the muddy and marshy places into the halls of wisdom and the royal roofs. Yet it spends its infancy among its own; for among those who do not understand it spiritually it is little, an infant, and has the food of sucklings. When it comes to the Church, Moses is stronger and more vigorous; for when the veil of the letter is removed, perfect food is found in the reading of it. She receives the wages of nursing from Pharao’s daughter, with whom the law is born and nursed. But what is it that the synagogue receives from the Church? I think it is what Moses says: “I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will anger you.” So the synagogue receives this wage from the Church: that it no longer worships idols. For seeing the Gentiles so turned to God that they no longer know idols, it blushes to worship idols any longer. We too, if we have had Pharao for a father, if he begot us in evil works, when we come to the waters, let us take up the law of God. Let not the letters seem foul to us like a dark covering; let us eat what in it is little and for sucklings; let us take up what is perfect and place it within the royal roofs of the heart. We have a great and strong Moses: let us think nothing small of him, nothing cheap, but all magnificent, all excellent, all goodly. For all that is spiritual and of lofty understanding is great.

04_marg1051: And when he was grown up, she delivered, etc. RABANUS. Josephus relates that Pharao’s daughter brought Moses, grown up, to her father, who set his crown on him; which Moses at once threw down, because he saw an image carved on it. Hence the priest who was there wished to kill him, saying that Egypt was to be overthrown through him, as he had learned from an oracle of the demons. But Pharao’s daughter freed him. And when he was of full age, he was sent by Pharao against the Ethiopians. And since he knew that he would march through deserts full of serpents, he took ibises, that is, Egyptian storks. And when he had pitched camp, he brought them out, so that they might devour and drive off the serpents; and so the army passed the night safely. So when he came to the city he was to storm, the queen of the Ethiopians fell in love with him, and by agreement handed the city over to him and married him. Hence it is that Aaron and Mary quarrelled with Moses on account of his Ethiopian wife.

04_marg1052: AUGUSTINE. For, as far as the Egyptians went, he was of a sonorous voice and of incomparable eloquence. But when he heard the voice of God and received the words of the Lord, he feels his voice thin and slight and slow, and his tongue hindered, and he declares himself dumb, when he begins to know the true Word, which was in the beginning with God. For though an untaught man be compared with dumb animals, he will seem eloquent; but compared with the learned and eloquent, foolish and dumb. But if anyone looks to the Word of God and the divine wisdom, he will profess himself a dumb animal before God far more than the cattle are before us. Hence: “I am become as a beast before thee.” So because he advanced so far in understanding as to know himself, which is a great part of wisdom, the divine favour rewards him, saying: “I will open thy mouth,” etc. Blessed are those whose mouth God opens, that they may speak. Hence: “Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.” Likewise Paul says: “That speech may be given me, that I may open my mouth.” So God opens the mouth of those who speak the words of God. The devil opens the mouth of those who speak lies, false witness, buffoonery, filthiness, and of whisperers and detractors, and of those who speak idle words. Of Judas it is related that Satan entered into him and put it into his heart to betray him. So he opened his mouth, that he might speak with the Pharisees how he should betray him for money received. And it is no small grace to tell apart the mouth that God opens and the one the devil opens. God also opens the ears of the saints to hear the divine words. Hence: “The Lord will open my ear”; he will open the eyes, as he “opened the eyes” of Agar, and she saw “a well of living water.” Hence Eliseus: “Open, Lord, the eyes of thy servant, that he may see, for there are more with us.” But the ear that is opened through the Lord’s instruction is sometimes open, sometimes shut. Hence: “Thou shalt not receive a vain report.” If vain, profane, filthy things are said, he who knows the Lord’s instruction shuts his ear and says: “But I, as a deaf man, heard not: and as a dumb man not opening his mouth.” But if what is said bears on the good of the soul, if the talk is of God, if it teaches morals, invites to virtues, cuts away vices, let the ears be open and the whole door of the soul. And note that the law used the greatest restraint in saying, “Thou shalt not receive a vain report.” It did not say “thou shalt not hear,” but “thou shalt not receive.” For we often hear vain things: Marcion and Valentius, and all who argue against the Creator, speak vain things; yet we often hear them, in order to answer them, but we do not receive them, because the devil opens their mouth. May the Lord deign to open our mouth, that we may be able to refute the gainsayer and stop the mouth that the devil opens.

For he had said: “I will open thy mouth and instruct thee.” But now he says: “I will open thy mouth and his mouth, and will instruct you in what you shall do.” But because he added, “and he shall speak for thee to the people,” the opening of the mouth seems to have been granted because Moses said he was slower of tongue. But as to the thinness of his voice the Lord willed to grant him nothing, but for this he added the help of his brother, who with a fitting voice would be equal to teaching the people. And when he says, “And thou shalt put my words in his mouth,” he shows that he would give them by speaking. For if only by hearing, as he would speak into the ears of the people; then what he says after, “And he shall speak for thee to the people, and he shall be thy mouth,” here too “to the people” is understood. And when he says “he shall speak for thee to the people,” he points to the leadership in Moses, the ministry in Aaron. They speak the truth, though they do not know it; as Caiphas, who said, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people,” did not know what he was saying. For as the Apostle says, “We are the good odour of Christ, to some unto life, to others unto death,” so the prophetic word is a sweet savour to believers; but to the doubtful and unbelieving, and to those who confess themselves Pharao’s people, it becomes an accursed savour. Moses himself too says to the Lord: “Since I spoke with Pharao, thou hast afflicted thy people”; because before the word of God is heard, there is no tribulation or temptation; but when the trumpet of preaching has given the signal of war, the battle of tribulations arises. So from the time Moses and Aaron began to speak to Pharao, the people of God is afflicted. From the time the word of God was brought forth into your soul, a struggle of the virtues against the vices is stirred up within you, which before lasted in peace within you. But when the word of God began to make the division in each one, a great disturbance arises, and war is born without treaty, because injustice does not agree with justice, nor drunkenness with sobriety, nor a lie with the truth. So let us not be troubled if we seem an accursed savour to Pharao. For virtue is called the execration of vice. But as Moses stood before Pharao, let us too stand, let us not be bent, having our loins girt about with truth, and our feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace. And we stand confidently if we pray the Lord to set our feet upon a firm rock, lest our feet be moved. Let us stand, that is, resist, according to that: “Whom resist ye, strong in faith,” that Satan may soon be crushed under our feet. For the more steadily and bravely we stand, the weaker Pharao is. But if we begin to be weak or doubtful, he will become stronger. For when Moses lifted up his hands, Amalec was overcome; when he let them drop as if tired, he prevailed. So let us lift up our arms in the power of the cross of Christ, and raise holy hands in prayer, that we may deserve the help of God. Hence James says: “Resist the devil, and he will fly from you.” So let us act so that he not only flees but is crushed under our feet: so Pharao was destroyed in the depth of the abyss. And we, if we go back out of the Egypt of the vices, escape the waves of the world as though on a solid road, through Jesus Christ.

04_marg1117: But I shall harden his heart, etc. AUGUSTINE. God says constantly, “I will harden Pharao’s heart,” and brings in as it were the cause why he does this: “I will harden Pharao’s heart, and I will fulfil my signs and my wonders in Egypt,” as if Pharao’s hardening were needed for the signs to be multiplied or fulfilled. So God makes good use of evil hearts, for what he wishes to show to the good and what he will do for the good. And although the quality of each heart in its malice, that is, what kind of heart it has toward evil, comes about by its own fault, which has grown up from its free choice, yet that this evil quality should be moved this way or that, whether it is moved wickedly this way or that, comes about through causes by which the mind of man is driven on; and whether these exist or not is not in man’s power, but they come from the hidden providence of God, who justly and wisely orders and governs all that he created. So that Pharao had such a heart that the patience of God did not move him to piety but rather to impiety was his own fault; but that those things were done which his heart, so malignant by its own fault, resisted, the commands of God (for this is what is called hardened, because it did not consent pliably but resisted unbendingly), was of the divine dispensation, by which a plainly just penalty was prepared for such a heart, by which those who fear God might be corrected. For when a gain is set before them (for example) for which a murder might be committed, the greedy man is moved one way, the despiser of money another: the one to commit the crime, the other to beware of it. Yet the setting forth of the gain was not in their power. So causes come to the wicked which are not in their power, but they make of them what the causes find them already made by their own vices, of their own will. “I will harden” can also be taken thus: I will show how hard it is.

04_marg1129: But … devoured, etc. AUGUSTINE. If it had been said, “Aaron’s dragon swallowed their rods,” it would be understood that Aaron’s true dragon swallowed not phantom feignings but rods. For it could swallow what they were, not what they seemed and were not. But because it said, “Aaron’s rod swallowed their rods,” a dragon could swallow rods, not a rod. But the thing is called by the name of what it was turned from, because it was also turned back into it. So it ought to be called what it principally was. What then is to be said of the magicians’ rods? Had they become true dragons, but are called rods by a like reason? Or rather did they seem to be what they were not, by a sorcerous mockery? Why then are they called rods and dragons on both sides, so that the manner of speaking differs nothing about those feignings? But it is hard to show. How, even if true dragons were made from the magicians’ rods, were they nonetheless not creators of dragons, neither the magicians nor the evil angels by whose ministry those things were done? For in bodily things, through all the elements of the world, there are certain hidden seminal reasons, which, when a fitting time is given them, break forth into their due kinds, according to their own measures and ends. And those who do such things are not called creators of the animals, as farmers are not creators of crops or trees or the like, though they furnish certain visible occasions and causes for their springing up. And what these do visibly, the angels do invisibly. But God alone is the true creator, who put those very causes and seminal reasons into things.
04_marg1130: And … was hardened, etc. God hardened Pharao’s heart because he so hardened the devil after his sin that he is never softened by the compunction of repentance; as it is said in Job: “His heart shall be as hard as a stone.”
04_interl2603: hence: “His heart shall be as hard as a stone.”
04_interl2604: for whom it ought to have been softened
04_interl2605: Eagerly, and as it were in the early morning, the devil is to be attacked.
04_marg1131: Behold he will go out, etc. ORIGEN. At first Moses does not go in to Pharao, but meets him going out to the waters; afterwards he goes in; after this he does not go in, but comes when summoned. Because, whether we have a contest with Pharao over the word of God and the defence of religion, or try to rescue souls besieged by him, and there is a struggle in us in disputing, we ought not at the first onset to go in to the last points of the questions, but must meet the adversary, even at his own waters, that is, the authorities of the Gentile philosophers, so as first to refute them and show that they have erred; then go into the inner parts of the contest. For the Lord says: “Unless a man first bind the strong man, he cannot enter into his house and rifle his goods.” So the strong man must first be bound and tied with the bonds of questions, and so we must go in to plunder the goods and free the souls which he had held by deceit and fraud. And when we have done this often and have stood against him, with our loins girt about with truth, standing in the Lord and acting manfully, the old and crafty artificer will pretend to be beaten and to give way, so as to make us more careless for the contest. He will also feign repentance; he will beg us to go away, but not far: he wants us to be near him in some part. But unless we go far from him, and cross the sea, and say in thought, speech and deed, “As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our iniquities from us,” we cannot be saved. So let us pray the mercy of God, that he may rescue us too from the land of Egypt, from the power of darkness, and sink Pharao with his army like lead in the mighty waters; and that we, set free, may with joy and gladness “sing a hymn to the Lord: for he is gloriously magnified,” etc.
04_interl2613: “Offer to God the sacrifice of praise.”
04_interl2616: as if it were in his choice either to hold or to let go
04_interl2619: in which they killed the little ones of the Hebrews, so that they may drink the blood they shed
04_marg1132: Behold I will strike, etc. ISIDORE. The plagues were done bodily in Egypt, but they are done spiritually in us. For Egypt is the figure of the world.
04_marg1133: The water of the river, and it shall be turned into, etc. STRABO. The water turned into blood signifies worldly wisdom, in which everyone who remains is killed, as a fish in blood. For worldly wisdom thinks it foolish that God should die for men: so whoever clings to it cannot live.
04_marg1134: The water of the river is turned into blood, to which they had handed over the boys of the Hebrews to be killed, so that it might give back a draught of blood to the authors of the crime, and they might taste by drinking the gore of the polluted stream which they had stained with parricidal slaughter. Allegorically too, the waters of Egypt are the wandering and slippery doctrines of the philosophers, which deceived those little in sense and understanding; but when the cross of Christ showed the light of truth, the slaughter of their own is required of them in punishment and the guilt of blood. Hence: “All the blood that hath been shed upon the earth shall be required of this generation.”
04_interl2623: hence: “All the blood that hath been shed upon the earth shall be required of this generation.”
04_marg1135: And it was turned, etc. RABANUS. The first commandment is about worshipping one God: “Thou shalt not have strange gods before me”; the first plague, water turned into blood. Compare the first commandment with the first plague: water, from which all things are produced, signifies the one God, from whom are all things; blood, mortal flesh. So the water was turned into blood, because they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man; and this change indeed takes place in the heart of the ungodly.
04_marg1136: Into blood, etc. Because those who think carnally about the causes of things are reproved by corrections of this kind, so that from the quality of the punishments they may recognize their error.
04_marg1137: AUGUSTINE. Pharao’s heart seems to have been hardened because the enchanters of the Egyptians did the like. But what follows teaches how great that hardening was, even when the enchanters failed.
04_marg1138: And all the Egyptians dug, etc. Because the Gentile world, confounded in its study of worldly philosophy, when it sees that there is nothing life-giving or wholesome in it, is eager, searching round about, seeking a draught of wisdom, and does not find it until it comes to him who said: “If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink.”
04_interl2628: A graceful expression, so that the frogs themselves are understood to be the plague.
04_marg1139: STRABO. There are three kinds of frogs. One lives in rivers and croaks. The second is very small, which is called the reed frog, of which it is said that if it is thrown into the mouth of a barking dog, it at once falls silent. The third is very large, which is called the bramble frog, very bad and poisonous, which is commonly called crassantium.
04_marg1140: The frogs signify the songs of the poets, which with an empty and puffed-up melody, as with the sounds and songs of frogs, brought fables of deceit into the world: for that animal is useful for nothing except that it gives out the sound of its voice in shameless and wearisome cries.
04_marg1141: The second commandment: “Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain.” The name of God is truth; for he himself says: “I am the truth.” He who speaks the truth speaks of God; for he who speaks a lie speaks of his own. For to speak truth is to speak reasonably; to speak vanity is to make a din. So the second commandment is about the love of truth, to which the love of iniquity is contrary. Truth speaks, vanity makes a din. Contrary to this is the second plague, the abundance of frogs, whose chatter signifies vanity. The lovers of truth do not take the name of God in vain, because they do not go back from truth into vanity. But those who contradict the truth and, deceived by vanity, deceive, are frogs, bringing weariness to the ears, not food to the minds. Hear men speaking reasonably: “There are no speeches nor languages, where their voices are not heard.” Hear the frogs: “They have spoken vain things, every one to his neighbour.”
04_marg1142: And the magicians also did, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked from where, if it had already been done everywhere. But the question is like this one: from where did they turn water into blood, if all the water of Egypt had already been turned into blood? But it is to be understood that the region where the children of Israel lived was not struck with such plagues, and from there the enchanters could draw water to turn into blood, or bring out frogs to show off their magic power; although they could also have done it after those things were finished; but Scripture, in its narrative, joined what could have happened afterwards.
04_interl2630: scourged, he comes to his senses, who before said: “I know not the Lord.”
04_interl2631: so that the frogs may be understood to have left Egypt by our prayer, not by chance
04_interl2632: in the flowing, that is, the filth of the world
04_interl2634: the feignings of the poets destroyed
04_marg1143: And Pharao seeing, etc. AUGUSTINE. Here it appears that Pharao was hardened not only because the enchanters did the like, but also because of the very patience of God, by which he spared; which, according to the hearts of men, is useful to some for repenting, useless to others, for resisting God and persevering in evil. Yet it is not useless in itself, but according to the evil heart; according to that: “Knowest thou not that the patience of God leadeth thee to penance? But according to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up to thyself wrath,” etc. For when the Apostle said elsewhere, “We are the good odour of Christ” in every place, he added: “in them that are saved, and in them that perish.” He did not say he was a good odour of Christ to those who are saved, but a bad one to those who perish; he called himself only a good odour. But they are such as to perish by a good odour according to the quality of their heart, which is to be changed by a good will in the grace of God, so that the judgments of God, which harm evil hearts, may begin to profit it. Hence he, his heart changed for the better, sang: “My soul shall live, and shall praise thee: and thy judgments shall help me.” He did not say “thy gifts” or “thy rewards,” but “thy judgments.”
04_marg1144: Moses chastising Egypt with the rod signifies the law, which reproves the world with the ten plagues of the commandments. The rod too, by which Egypt is reproved and Pharao overcome, is the cross of Christ, by which the world is conquered and the devil overcome or triumphed over. The rod cast down becomes a serpent, which signifies wisdom, according to that: “Be ye wise as serpents,” etc. The rod devoured the serpents of the magicians, and the cross of Christ, whose preaching seems folly, overcomes all the wisdom of the world. Hence: “For he wrote of me.” The rod cast on the ground was turned into a serpent, because when the mystery of the cross came to the faith of men, it made the wisdom of the world foolish.
04_interl2635: the subtleties of dialectic, or the heretics who deceive the unlearned with dialectical syllogisms
04_marg1145: ORIGEN. This animal is held up on wings, flying through the air, but so fine and tiny that it escapes the sight of the eye, unless one sees sharply. Yet when it has settled on the body, it bores with a most bitter sting, so that one who cannot see it flying feels it stinging. So this animal is compared to the art of dialectic, which bores into souls with tiny and subtle stings of words, and gets round them with such cunning that the one deceived neither sees nor understands by what he is deceived.
04_marg1146: The third commandment: “Remember to keep holy the sabbath day.” By this is suggested the rest and tranquillity of mind that a good conscience makes. There is sanctification, because there is the Spirit of God. Hence: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, but upon the humble and quiet?” etc. So the restless spring back from the Holy Spirit, the stirrers of quarrels, the lovers of slanders, and they do not admit the rest of the spiritual sabbath. So be gentle; let there be no tumult in your heart, with phantasms flying about through corruption and stinging you. Hear God saying: “Be still and see that I am God.” You will not be still because of your restlessness, and, blinded, you demand to see what you cannot. For mark the contrary plague: the sciniphs were born in the land of Egypt from the mud, very tiny flies, most restless, flying without order, rushing into the eyes and denying men rest; when driven off, they come back: so are the phantasms of the restless. Keep the commandment, beware the plague.
04_interl2636: they tried to do it, that is, by stretching out their hands holding rods
04_marg1147: The blood is the teaching of the philosophers; the frogs, the feignings of the poets; the sciniphs, the sophisms of the dialecticians: all of which deceived the world.
04_interl2637: the Spirit, who gives the divisions of graces
04_marg1148: The finger of God, etc. ISIDORE. At the third sign the magicians fail, saying, “It is the finger of God”; they bore the type and the animosity of the heretics. Hence: “As Jamnes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith,” etc. And these, who were restless through corruption of mind, failed at the third sign, confessing that the Holy Spirit, who was in Moses, was against them. For the Spirit, who is the finger of God, is put in the third place: who, as when appeased he gives rest to the meek and humble of heart, so when angered he harries the unmeek and proud through restlessness, which the most grievous flies signified, under which the magicians failed, saying, “This is the finger of God,” lest they should understand by what they are deceived.
04_marg1149: Note that the magicians were overcome at the third sign, because all faithlessness and worldly wisdom or philosophy is overcome by faith in the Trinity. For though they found philosophy and disputed about the frame of the whole world, they could not come to the knowledge of the Trinity. By the finger the Holy Spirit is understood, not because he is less than the Father and the Son, but because in the finger there are very many divisions, and through the Holy Spirit the division of graces is given.
04_marg1150: When the magicians said to Pharao, “This is the finger of God,” because they could not bring forth sciniphs, they perceived (since they knew the power of their wicked arts) that they had been thwarted not by such arts, as if Moses were more powerful in them, but by the finger of God, who worked through Moses, who is the Holy Spirit. For what one evangelist says, “by the finger of God,” another set out as “by the Spirit of God.” So when the magicians, in whose power Pharao trusted, confessed that the finger of God was in Moses, by which their sorceries are overcome, yet Pharao’s heart was hardened. But why the magicians failed at the third plague is hard to perceive and explain. For they could have failed at the first sign, where the rod was turned into a serpent, and at the first plague, where the water was turned into blood, and at the second, of the frogs, if the finger, that is, the Spirit, of God had willed it. For who would say that the magicians could be hindered by the finger of God at this sign, and not at the earlier ones? So there is certainly a reason why they were allowed to do those things up to this point. For perhaps the Trinity is commended; and, what is true, the greatest philosophers of the Gentiles, as far as is traced in their writings, philosophized without the Holy Spirit, though they were not silent about the Father and the Son.
04_interl2643: Resist the devil, and he will fly from you.
04_interl2644: the flowing of the world, that is, which Pharao loves; or the peoples, whom he easily deceives
04_marg1151: Thus saith the Lord, etc. RABANUS. The fourth commandment: “Honour thy father and thy mother.” Contrary to this is the fourth plague, that is, the cinomia, the dog fly: it is doglike not to acknowledge one’s parents. Hence their whelps are born blind.
04_marg1152: ISIDORE. In the fourth place Egypt is struck with flies. Now the fly is an insolent and restless animal, in which the insolent cares of carnal desires are figured. And Egypt is struck with flies because the hearts of those who love the world are struck with the restlessness of desires. The Septuagint put cynomia, that is, the dog fly, by which doglike manners are signified, in which the lust of the human mind and the desire of the flesh are reproved. The eloquence of men in the courts can also be signified by the dog fly: they tear one another like dogs.
04_marg1153: The cinomia is the sect of the heretics who, besides their other wickednesses of deceit, preach pleasure and lust as the highest good. So since the world was first deceived by each of these things, the word and law of God, coming, rightly reproves it with corrections of this kind, so that from the quality of the punishments they may know the quality of their own error.
04_marg1154: And I will make … wonderful, etc. AUGUSTINE. This is to be understood to have been done in the earlier signs too, so that the land in which the people of God lived was troubled by no such plagues. But it was fitting that it be set down plainly here. For from here begin the signs whose like the magicians did not try to do. For it is certain that there were sciniphs everywhere in Pharao’s kingdom, but not in the land of Gessen or Gesem. There the magicians tried to do the like, and could not; so until they failed, nothing was said about the separation of that land; but only from when those things began to be done which they would not even dare to try.
04_interl2648: The rush and crowd of thoughts that meet us most of all at prayer.
04_interl2651: by doglike manners, by troublesome thoughts
04_marg1155: And there came a … fly, etc. AUGUSTINE. “Fly” is put for a multitude of flies. For I do not know how, through the custom of speaking that has steeped men’s senses, what is said in the singular often seems more than what is said in the plural. For example, “there is soldiery there” means more than “there are soldiers there”; “there is fish there” means more than “there are fishes there.”
04_interl2652: Egypt, that is: he did not want them to go where they said, lest they go far from him.
04_interl2653: For the Egyptians disdain to eat sheep.
04_marg1156: The abominations, etc. The wicked Egyptians abominate good things; that is, the citizens of this world abominate the sheep, that is, the simplicity of the good: for as the good abominate evil things, so the evil abominate good. Hence the good abominate an ungodly man, and the ungodly those who are in the right way.
04_marg1157: The Egyptians disdain to eat sheep; but what the Egyptians abominate the Israelites offer to God, because the simplicity of conscience which the unjust despise as lowest and most abject, the just turn into a sacrifice of virtue; and cultivating the purity and meekness of what is right, they sacrifice to God what the reprobate, abominating it, think folly.
04_marg1158: Moses said that he wished to go into the desert, where the Egyptians would not see their abominations. And this is to be understood as mystically signified, as we said of the shepherds who were abominable to the Egyptians, and so the Israelites received a separate land in Egypt. For so the sacrifices of the Israelites are abominations to the Egyptians, as the life of the just is to the wicked.
04_marg1159: The Egyptians abominate sheep, and worship them because of Jove Hammon, who is painted with a ram’s head. Likewise the Egyptians worship the ox, which is consecrated to Apis, as the cow to Isis. For Apis was the greatest god of the Egyptians, who appeared once a year at a fixed time to their priests. And they, following him with hymns and praises, prophesied as if frenzied.
04_marg1160: Egypt is struck with flies. Nothing is more toilsome than to burn with earthly desires; nothing more restful than to desire nothing in the world. So Israel receives the keeping of the sabbath as a gift; Egypt is struck with a multitude of flies. For he who follows God receives the sabbath, that is, rest of mind, so as not to be wearied by the craving of carnal desire. But Egypt, that is, the world, is struck with flies, that is, with the insolent cares of desires. Hence: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the ointment,” because the superfluous thoughts which are constantly born and die in a mind thinking carnal things spoil the sweetness with which each one is anointed within by the Spirit, because they do not let him enjoy it whole. Hence, when the crowd had been put out, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl arose. So the crowd is put out so that the girl may be raised, because first the multitude of cares is driven from the secret places of the heart, and so the soul that lies dead within will rise. For while each one scatters himself through countless thoughts of desires, he does not gather himself to the knowledge of himself. For no one fully receives the wisdom which is God unless he draws himself back from all the tossing of carnal thoughts. Hence: “Write wisdom in the time of leisure: and he that is less in action shall receive it.” And again: “Be still and see that I am God.”
04_marg1161: And … was hardened, etc. AUGUSTINE. When the locust had been taken away, it was said of Pharao: “Pharao hardened his heart, even at this time, and would not let the people go.” Certainly now it is not said, “Pharao’s heart was hardened,” but, “Pharao hardened his heart.” As indeed in all the plagues, the origin of vices is from the will of man. So the hearts of men are moved by causes, some in this way, others in that, often in different ways even by causes that are not different, according to their own qualities, which come from their wills.
